## Overview

This blog post explores the ["How to Lead a
Team"](https://abseil.io/resources/swe-book/html/ch05.html) chapter from
[*Software Engineering at Google*](https://abseil.io/resources/swe-book),
written by Brian Fitzpatrick. After earlier chapters on team culture, this
chapter discusses the people who work to help a team succeed: its leaders.
The chapter compares a team without a leader to a boat without a captain.
It may keep moving, but it drifts without a clear direction. Even for
engineers who never plan to manage anyone, understanding good leadership helps
them work better with their own leaders and guide their own projects.

## Summary

Google recognizes two leadership roles: a manager, who leads people, and a
tech lead, who leads the technical work. Both roles require planning, but they
call for different people skills. The chapter argues that leading a team is a
different job from writing software, so strong engineers do not automatically
become strong managers. Good leaders move away from traditional command-style
management and focus on serving their team. They delegate whenever they can,
remove obstacles, and keep the team focused on the right goals while
protecting it from outside distractions. The sections below cover how
engineers move into leadership, what today's engineering managers do, which
habits help or harm a team, and how leaders can support each person's
motivation and growth.

### Managers & Tech Leads

Engineering leadership includes two closely connected roles. An engineering manager
supports the team's performance, productivity, and well-being while balancing
individual needs with the goals of the business. A tech lead focuses on the
technical direction of the product, including architecture, technology choices,
priorities, and project coordination. Together, they help engineers find work
that matches their abilities and gives them opportunities to grow.

On smaller teams, one person may fill both roles as a Tech Lead Manager (TLM).
This requires balancing technical contributions with delegation and people
management, which can be difficult for someone moving from an individual
contributor role. Larger teams at Google generally divide these responsibilities
between two people so each can give their work enough attention. Across these
roles, effective leadership depends on helping other people succeed. A tech
lead who delegates a task, even when completing it personally would be faster,
can build the team's skills and ability to work independently.

### Moving from an Individual Contributor Role to a Leadership Role

Every project needs someone to guide it, and that person is often an engaged
individual contributor who gradually starts settling disagreements, making
decisions, and coordinating teammates. The chapter calls this drift
"manageritis". Even engineers who insist they will never manage can end up
leading after doing their work well. The chapter does not try to convince
readers to become managers. Instead, it explains how good leaders serve their
teams through humility, respect, and trust, so that anyone can understand
leadership well enough to guide their own work.

Many engineers are hesitant to take on a leadership role, and the chapter
identifies several common reasons:

- **Less time coding:** Writing code produces visible results each day, while
  management work is harder to measure and its benefits take longer to appear.
  New leaders can feel unproductive even when their team is doing well.
- **The Peter Principle:** *“In a hierarchy every employee tends to rise to*
  *his level of incompetence.”* People tend to be promoted until they reach a
  role they cannot perform well. Google tries to avoid this by expecting people
  to work above their current level for a time before they are promoted.
- **Bad past managers:** Engineers who have mostly worked for poor managers may
  have little desire to become one, as they've never had a model for what to
  do that would be successful.

The chapter also offers reasons to consider leading. An individual's output is
limited, but guiding a team allows a person to have a much larger impact.
People who step in when a team lacks direction often discover that they are
good at helping and protecting others. Google asserts that someone has to lead,
and a capable engineer is often the right person to do it.

#### Servant Leadership

New managers sometimes repeat the habits of the bad managers they once worked
for, such as micromanaging, ignoring low performers, or hiring people who will
not challenge them. The author recalls a Google mentor that told him,
*"Above all, resist the urge to manage."* The urge to "manage" is often,
according to the chapter, the new leader's most harmful instinct. It offers the
alternative: servant leadership, where the leader's main job is to support
the team. In practice, this means building an environment of humility,
respect, and trust; clearing obstacles the team cannot remove alone; helping
the group reach consensus; offering small kindnesses; and staying involved in
the work when needed. A servant leader looks after both the technical and the
social health of the team, and the social side, though harder to manage, is
just as important.

### The Engineering Manager

The common image of a rigid, controlling manager goes back to military
hierarchies and to factories in the Industrial Revolution. Factory workers
could be trained quickly and replaced easily, so supervisors relied on a
"carrot-and-stick" approach: reward people who comply and punish those who
do not. Google says that Software engineering is different. Engineers working
on large codebases can need months to become productive, and creative work
requires time, support, and room to think. Research suggests that
carrot-and-stick management actually hurts this kind of work.

Today's engineering managers are more effective when they trust their teams.
When people can see that their manager trusts them, they feel *"a positive*
*pressure to live up to that trust."*" The chapter's key distinction is that
traditional managers focus on *how* work gets done, while great managers focus
on *what* gets done and let the team decide how to do it.

#### Failure Is an Option

Leaders should also create psychological safety, an environment where team
members can be themselves and take risks without fearing their manager's or
peers' reactions. People are poor at judging risk, and organizations often
settle for small, safe wins. Aiming for an ambitious goal may fail, but it
usually produces far more than a conservative target. Failure is acceptable as
long as the team learns from it and avoids repeating the same mistake.

Not all failures cost the same. Failing fast is cheap, failing slowly wastes
engineering time, and failures that reach customers are the most expensive.
After major failures, Google teams write postmortems that explain what
happened and how to prevent it from happening again. The goal is to fix the
underlying problem rather than assign blame. The chapter also recommends
praising individuals in public, giving individual criticism in private, and
treating failures as learning opportunities for the whole team.

### Antipatterns

The chapter describes several leadership antipatterns: habits that undermine
trust, weaken collaboration, and make a team less effective. Recognizing these
habits helps leaders understand how their own decisions affect the people
around them.

- **Hiring pushovers:** Choosing people who will never challenge the leader
  limits the team's independence. Strong teammates bring different ideas,
  question mistakes, and can eventually take on leadership responsibilities.
- **Ignoring low performers:** Avoiding difficult conversations leaves other
  team members carrying extra work and allows frustration to grow. Leaders
  should address problems early through respectful coaching, clear
  expectations, and small, measurable goals.
- **Ignoring human issues:** Technical progress depends on people whose needs
  and circumstances vary. A leader who dismisses personal challenges can lose
  the team's trust, even when the work itself is going well.
- **Trying to be everyone's friend:** A manager's influence over people's
  careers changes the relationship. Leaders can remain approachable and
  supportive while maintaining boundaries and making fair decisions.
- **Compromising the hiring bar:** Filling positions quickly can create lasting
  problems if candidates do not meet the requirements of the role. Maintaining
  hiring standards protects the team's time and ability to succeed.
- **Treating the team like children:** Constant supervision and unnecessary
  restrictions discourage ownership. Giving capable engineers responsibility
  shows trust and allows them to develop their judgment.

These antipatterns show why humility, respect, and trust matter in everyday
leadership. A leader needs to listen, address problems directly, and give
people enough support and independence to do their work well.

### Positive Patterns

The chapter also describes positive patterns: practices the authors have seen
in effective leaders at Google, in other leaders they have observed, and in
their own mentors. These habits help leaders earn trust, keep the team moving,
and give people room to grow.

- **Lose the ego:** Humility does not mean a lack of confidence. Leaders can
  hold strong opinions while building a shared team identity, trusting the
  people closest to the work, welcoming criticism, and apologizing sincerely
  when they make mistakes.
- **Be a Zen master:** Teams take emotional cues from their leader, so staying
  calm and avoiding excessive cynicism matters. Answering questions with
  questions helps teammates reach their own solutions and keep ownership.
- **Be a catalyst:** Leaders often move work forward by building consensus
  rather than relying on authority. A team may choose to let its lead make
  quick decisions, and leaders do not need complete agreement before acting.
- **Remove roadblocks:** When the team is stuck on a technical or
  organizational problem, the leader steps in to get it moving. Knowing the
  right person to ask is often more valuable than knowing the answer.
- **Be a teacher and a mentor:** Leaders should let junior engineers learn by
  doing a task, even when it would be faster to do it themselves. Good mentors
  explain clearly and judge how much help someone needs without
  over-explaining.
- **Set clear goals:** A concise mission statement, clear priorities, and
  guidance on trade-offs keep everyone moving in the same direction. Once the
  goals are set, the leader can step back and only check in periodically.
- **Be honest:** Leaders should admit when they do not know something or
  cannot share information. Difficult feedback should be specific, private,
  and respectful rather than hidden inside a "compliment sandwich," where the
  criticism is easy to miss.
- **Track happiness:** Leaders should watch for burnout, recognize good work,
  and share thankless tasks fairly. Asking what people need and making their
  career goals explicit helps leaders offer useful support.

These patterns share a common thread: a leader's main job is to support the
people doing the work. By staying humble, honest, and focused on clear goals,
leaders create a team where people can do their best work and grow over time.

### The Unexpected Question

The author, Fitzpatrick, describes preparing for difficult questions before his first
meeting with then-CEO Eric Schmidt. Instead, Schmidt ended the meeting by
asking whether Fitzpatrick needed anything. The question caught him off guard
because he had prepared to defend his work rather than ask for support.

This example shows how a simple question can put servant leadership into
practice. Asking team members what they need creates an opportunity to discuss
obstacles, missing resources, or concerns that might otherwise stay hidden.
Asking regularly during one-on-one meetings gives people time to recognize
their needs and become more comfortable sharing them.

These conversations can also help leaders understand job satisfaction and
career goals. Someone may want to learn a skill, take on more responsibility,
or receive recognition for work that has gone unnoticed. Leaders should also
recognize that circumstances outside work can affect a person's capacity,
while respecting their privacy. Listening and following through on these
conversations helps turn concern for the team into useful support.

### Other Tips & Tricks

The chapter offers several practical habits for supporting a team. Delegation
is especially important because it gives others opportunities to learn and
prevents the leader from becoming a bottleneck. Leaders should also stay
involved enough to understand the work. Taking on an unpleasant task can show
commitment and help a leader learn what the team is dealing with.

Developing future leaders is another responsibility. Giving interested team
members opportunities to coordinate work or make decisions prepares them to
take on more responsibility. This should account for individual interests:
engineers who prefer to remain individual contributors also need meaningful
opportunities to grow.

Leaders must also address difficult situations before they damage the team.
Delaying a conversation about performance or disruptive behavior usually makes
the problem harder to resolve. At the same time, leaders should protect the
team's focus by handling unnecessary outside demands and sharing relevant
organizational information without passing along every uncertainty.

Finally, effective leaders recognize good work and make room for experiments.
Specific praise helps people understand the value of their contributions.
When a proposed experiment is easy to reverse and fits the team's priorities,
giving it a chance can encourage learning. Decisions that create lasting
commitments deserve more careful consideration.

### People Are Like Plants

The author's mother-in-law, who raised six very children, compared kids to
plants when he asked her how she "managed" it. Some need little water and
lots of sun, others need shade and damp soil, and some do best with fertilizer.
Treating them all the same means none of them gets what they need. Team members
work the same way, and a leader's job is to learn what each person needs. On
a team, the two main inputs are motivation and direction. Someone stuck in
a rut needs motivation, someone distracted or unsure of what to do needs
direction, and someone who feels adrift may need both. Giving either one to a
person who does not need it can be frustrating for them.

Direction is fairly simple to provide: understand what needs to be done,
organize the work, and break it into manageable tasks. Motivation is more
complicated.

#### Intrinsic Versus Extrinsic Motivation

Extrinsic motivation comes from outside a person, such as a paycheck, while
intrinsic motivation comes from within. Drawing on Dan Pink's book *Drive*,
Google argues that the best way to motivate people is to strengthen their
intrinsic motivation. Pink identifies three sources of it:

- **Autonomy:** People work better when they are not micromanaged. A leader
  can set the general direction and let the team decide how to get there,
  which gives people a real stake in the product and a sense of ownership.
- **Mastery:** People need chances to improve their skills and learn new ones.
  Like a knife that dulls without sharpening, skills fade without practice,
  and a team grows stronger when its members keep learning.
- **Purpose:** Work is more motivating when people understand why it matters.
  Even a product with modest impact can inspire a team when leaders connect
  the work to the people it helps. One manager shared customer emails praising
  the product with the engineers, which raised morale and led to new ideas.

Money still matters, but the chapter treats it as a baseline: people should be
paid well enough that income is not a source of stress. Beyond that point,
autonomy, mastery, and purpose do far more to keep a team engaged.

### Reflection

As future software engineers, we can apply these ideas before holding a formal
leadership title. In a class project, leadership might mean clarifying the
next milestone, helping a teammate work through a blocker, or making space for
someone whose ideas have not been heard. These actions help the group move
forward while building trust.

One lesson we can take from this chapter is to reconsider how we measure our
contributions. Completing a difficult feature matters, but helping another
person understand the code or take ownership of a task can strengthen the
whole team. Doing everything ourselves may produce a quick result while
leaving teammates without opportunities to learn.

In our next group project, we can put these lessons into practice by asking
what support each person needs, agreeing on clear responsibilities, and
addressing concerns early. We can also recognize each other's contributions
and share opportunities to lead. The chapter encourages us to see leadership
as an ongoing responsibility to help people grow and work effectively together.
